lead: Resistive transducers turn displacement, strain, temperature, light or magnetic field into a change of resistance, which is then read as a voltage. After this unit you can pick the right resistive sensor for a job, compute its output for a given input, design the divider or bridge that reads it, and correct the errors — loading, self-heating, lead resistance, cold junction — that would otherwise spoil the reading.
about: Unit 2 covers the family of sensors whose resistance changes when something physical changes. Chapter 2.1 starts with the potentiometer, the simplest resistive displacement sensor. Chapter 2.2 explains the strain gauge, where a tiny stretch changes resistance, and how metal and semiconductor gauges differ. Chapter 2.3 bonds gauges to an elastic element to make load cells and torque shafts. Chapter 2.4 turns the same idea to temperature with RTDs and thermistors. Chapter 2.5 applies the temperature-sensitive wire to flow and to moisture, giving the hot-wire anemometer and the resistance hygrometer. Chapter 2.6 adds two more resistive families: photo-resistive and magneto-resistive sensors. Chapter 2.7 closes with the thermocouple, the one temperature sensor that generates its own emf and needs cold-junction compensation.

chapters.idea: A potentiometer converts linear or angular displacement into a resistance change, and a divider turns that into a voltage proportional to displacement.
chapters.depth: Construction of the track: wire-wound on a former, carbon film, conductive plastic. Linear, rotary, multi-turn and helical forms, with a wiper as the sliding contact. Define stroke L, supply V_s, and output V₀ = V_s·(x/L) for the unloaded case. Derive the loaded-divider expression and the loading error, and show the error is zero at both ends and largest near mid-stroke. Resolution equals the spacing between adjacent turns on a wire-wound unit and is effectively continuous on a film track. Cover linearity, wiper friction, wear, contact noise and life. Applications: machine-tool travel, servo feedback, volume control, Bourdon-tube pressure gauge. Some syllabi call this the variable-resistance transducer or the slider potentiometer.

figure.aria: Two curves of output voltage against slider position over a 100 mm stroke; the loaded curve sags below the straight ideal line and meets it only at the two ends.
figure.caption: The straight line is the ideal 10 V over 100 mm. The sagging curve is the same potentiometer feeding a 10 kΩ load: 4.00 V instead of 5.00 V at mid-stroke.

chapters.example: A wire-wound potentiometer has a total resistance of 10 kΩ, is fed from a 10 V d.c. supply and has a 100 mm stroke. (a) Find the ideal output at 50 mm. (b) Find the actual output when a 10 kΩ load is connected across the output. (c) Find the loading error. Answer: (a) V₀ = 10 × 50/100 = 5.00 V. (b) V₀ = 10 × (0.5)/(1 − 0.5² + 0.5) = 5/1.25 = 4.00 V. (c) 1.00 V low, that is 20 %.
chapters.trap: Ignoring the loading effect and quoting V_s·x/L as the real output. The divider only behaves linearly when the load resistance is far larger than the track resistance, so the load must be at least ten times the track.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for sensitivity, resolution and linearity as static characteristics.
chapters.leave: Wheatstone bridge circuits and buffer amplifiers to Unit 6; LVDT and other inductive position sensors to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: A strain gauge is a resistor whose resistance changes in proportion to the strain it is stretched by, with the gauge factor as the constant of proportionality.
chapters.depth: Define stress σ = F/A, strain ε = ΔL/L (dimensionless, quoted in microstrain µε = 10⁻⁶), and Young's modulus E = σ/ε. Poisson ratio ν gives the transverse contraction. Gauge factor GF = (ΔR/R)/ε = 1 + 2ν + (Δρ/ρ)/ε, so it has a geometric part and a piezoresistive part; some syllabi call it the k-factor. Metal foil gauges: constantan grid on a polyimide backing, GF about 2, nearly linear, self-temperature-compensated alloys, gauge lengths from 0.2 mm to 100 mm, bonded with cyanoacrylate. Semiconductor gauges: diffused silicon, GF of 50 to 200, p-type negative, far more sensitive but nonlinear and strongly temperature dependent. Wire the gauge into quarter, half or full bridge — quote the results only (quarter bridge output V_s·GF·ε/4, full bridge V_s·GF·ε) and leave the bridge itself to Unit 6. Cover transverse sensitivity, lead resistance, apparent strain and dummy-gauge compensation, rosettes for principal strains, and use as a displacement or diaphragm pressure transducer. Biomedical uses: bone and implant strain, diaphragm blood-pressure capsules, muscle-force and respiration belts.

figure.aria: Two straight lines of resistance change against strain, both starting at zero; the semiconductor line is fifty times steeper than the metal line.
figure.caption: At the same 500 µε the metal gauge changes resistance by 0.1 % and the semiconductor gauge by 5 %. The gain in sensitivity is paid for in nonlinearity and temperature drift.

chapters.example: A constantan foil gauge has R = 120 Ω and gauge factor 2.0. It is bonded to a steel member carrying a strain of 500 µε. (a) Find ΔR. (b) Find the percentage change. (c) Repeat for a silicon gauge with gauge factor 100 at the same strain. Answer: (a) ΔR = GF·ε·R = 2.0 × 500×10⁻⁶ × 120 Ω = 0.12 Ω. (b) 0.12/120 = 0.1 %. (c) ΔR = 100 × 500×10⁻⁶ × 120 Ω = 6.0 Ω, that is 5 %.
chapters.trap: Dropping the 10⁻⁶ in microstrain, or mixing up ε and ΔL/L. Also: a gauge factor of 2 is not a unit of resistance change — ΔR/R is dimensionless, so the same GF gives different ΔR for 120 Ω and 350 Ω gauges.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.1 for the change-of-resistance-to-voltage idea, and Unit 1 for sensitivity and linearity.
chapters.leave: Bridge balance, excitation and the instrumentation amplifier to Unit 6; piezoresistive MEMS diaphragms and semiconductor fabrication to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Bond strain gauges to a carefully shaped elastic element and the strain reading becomes a force, weight or torque reading.
chapters.depth: Element shapes: column (compression or tension), cantilever and double-bending beam, shear web, proving ring, S-type. Four active gauges in a full bridge give temperature compensation and four times the quarter-bridge output. Specify rated capacity, safe overload, ultimate overload, creep, hysteresis, non-linearity, and sensitivity in mV/V of excitation, typically about 2 mV/V. Overload stops and hermetic sealing. Compare briefly with hydraulic load cells and with capacitive and piezoelectric types, without teaching those. Torque: T = F·r and shaft power P = 2πNT/60 with T in N·m, N in rev/s, P in W. Torque shafts carry gauges at 45° to the axis in a full bridge; get the signal off the rotating shaft by slip rings, rotary transformer or FM telemetry, and mention reaction-torque measurement on a stationary frame. Applications: retail weighing scale, weighbridge, crane and hoist load limiting, motor and pump test beds, torque wrench calibration.

figure.aria: A chain of blocks from the applied load, through the elastic column and its strain, to the bonded gauges, the bridge output and the display.
figure.caption: The numbers are the worked example: the same 10 kN produces 159 µε on the column and only 1.59 mV out of the bridge, which is why an amplifier follows.

chapters.example: A compression load cell is a solid steel column of 20 mm diameter with E = 200 GPa. Four 120 Ω gauges of gauge factor 2.0 form a full bridge excited at 5 V. For a 10 kN load find the stress, the strain, ΔR per gauge and the bridge output. Answer: A = π(0.010 m)² = 3.142×10⁻⁴ m²; σ = 10 000 N / 3.142×10⁻⁴ m² = 31.8 MPa; ε = σ/E = 31.8×10⁶ / 200×10⁹ = 1.59×10⁻⁴ = 159 µε; ΔR = GF·ε·R = 2 × 1.59×10⁻⁴ × 120 Ω = 0.038 Ω; V_o = V_s·GF·ε = 5 V × 3.18×10⁻⁴ = 1.59 mV.
chapters.trap: Using the quarter-bridge formula for a four-gauge load cell, which under-reads by a factor of four. Also confusing rated capacity with safe overload, and forgetting that torque gauges must be aligned at 45° to the shaft axis, not along it.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.2 for gauge factor, bridge configurations and temperature compensation.
chapters.leave: Capacitive and piezoelectric load cells to Units 3 and 4; full bridge linearity, excitation and amplifier design to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: RTDs use a pure metal whose resistance rises steadily with temperature; thermistors use a ceramic whose resistance falls steeply and nonlinearly.
chapters.depth: RTD, also called a resistance temperature detector: platinum (Pt100 = 100 Ω at 0 °C, Pt1000), nickel and copper; platinum is the standard because it is stable, chemically inert and nearly linear. Linear law R_T = R₀(1 + αT) with α = 0.00385 /°C for platinum, plus the Callendar–Van Dusen form R_T = R₀[1 + AT + BT² + C(T − 100)T³] for wide ranges. Typical ranges: platinum −200 °C to 600 °C, nickel and copper for narrower, cheaper spans. Two-wire, three-wire and four-wire connections and the lead-resistance error each one leaves. Self-heating and the measurement current. Thermistor: sintered oxides of manganese, nickel, cobalt and iron; NTC and PTC; the β law R_T = R₀·exp[β(1/T − 1/T₀)] with T in kelvin and β typically 3000 K to 4000 K. Sensitivity of an NTC is about −3 %/°C to −5 %/°C, some ten times a Pt100, but over a small span, −50 °C to 150 °C, and nonlinear. Dissipation constant, time constant, interchangeability. Biomedical temperature sensing: skin and core probes to 0.1 °C, reused thermometer tips, and the self-heating limit that keeps the probe current small.

figure.aria: Two curves: the platinum line rises gently and almost straight from 1.0 to about 1.39, while the thermistor curve falls steeply from about 2.9 down to 0.09 over the same span.
figure.caption: Normalised so both start near 1: the platinum sensor moves a few tenths over 100 °C, the thermistor drops by a factor of thirty. The thermistor is far more sensitive and far less linear.

chapters.example: (a) Find the resistance of a Pt100 at 50 °C, taking α = 0.00385 /°C. (b) An NTC thermistor is 10 kΩ at 25 °C with β = 3500 K. Find its resistance at 37 °C. Answer: (a) R = 100(1 + 0.00385 × 50) = 119.25 Ω, a change of 19.25 Ω, so sensitivity = 0.385 Ω/°C, that is 0.385 %/°C. (b) T = 310.15 K, T₀ = 298.15 K; R = 10 000 × exp[3500 × (1/310.15 − 1/298.15)] = 10 000 × exp(−0.454) = 6.35 kΩ. That is 3.0 %/°C, about eight times the Pt100 sensitivity.
chapters.trap: Putting Celsius into the β equation. It needs absolute temperature, so add 273.15 first. Also: a two-wire RTD hides the lead resistance inside the reading, and a large measuring current heats the element above the temperature it is meant to measure.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for calibration, accuracy and zero/first-order response; Chapter 2.1 for reading a resistance as a voltage.
chapters.leave: Bridges, linearising circuits and transmitters to Unit 6; IC and semiconductor temperature sensors and general humidity sensing to Unit 5; thermocouples to Chapter 2.7.

chapters.idea: The resistance–temperature relation, applied to a tiny heated wire, measures flow speed, and a moisture-sensitive film's resistance measures humidity.
chapters.depth: Hot-wire anemometer: a platinum or tungsten wire a few micrometres across and a few millimetres long, heated above the flow temperature. Heat balance I²R = hA(T_w − T_a), and King's law h = a + b·u^0.5, which gives E² = A + B·u^n with n near 0.5 for the calibration curve. Two modes: constant current (the wire cools and its resistance drops) and constant temperature (a feedback amplifier holds the wire hot and the drive current becomes the output, giving the faster instrument). Temperature compensation with a cold wire, calibration, directional probes and hot-film versions for liquids. Applications: duct and wind-tunnel velocity, engine intake flow, turbulence, respiratory airflow. Resistance hygrometer: a hygroscopic film, a conductive polymer or a lithium-chloride layer on electrodes; water uptake raises ionic conduction, so resistance falls as relative humidity rises, roughly one decade per 30 % RH. Define relative humidity as the ratio of water vapour present to the saturation amount at that temperature, and distinguish it from absolute humidity and dew point. Typical range 10 % to 90 % RH, accuracy of a few percent, slow response, contamination and temperature dependence. Applications: textile and spinning mills, cold stores, weather stations, HVAC and grain storage.

figure.aria: A closed loop: flow cools the wire, the bridge senses the resistance change, an error amplifier drives more current back into the wire, and that same drive current is the flow output.
figure.caption: The dashed edge is the feedback that keeps the wire at constant temperature. The current needed to hold it hot is the measurement, so the instrument never drifts with ambient temperature alone.

chapters.example: A constant-temperature hot-wire anemometer obeys E² = A + B·u^0.5 with A = 4 V² and B = 2 V²/(m s⁻¹)^0.5. (a) Find E at 9 m/s. (b) Find u when E = 3.46 V. (c) A resistive hygrometer reads 1 MΩ at 30 % RH and 100 kΩ at 60 % RH. Assuming a log-linear law, find R at 45 % RH. Answer: (a) E² = 4 + 2 × 3 = 10, so E = 3.16 V. (b) E² = 12; 12 − 4 = 8 = 2√u, so √u = 4 and u = 16 m/s. (c) Half-way in RH is half-way in log R: R = 1 MΩ × 10^(−15/30) = 1 MΩ / 3.16 = 316 kΩ.
chapters.trap: Plotting E against u and expecting a straight line, when the calibration is linear only in E² against √u. On the humidity side, mistaking relative humidity for absolute humidity — a resistive hygrometer reading changes with temperature even when the water vapour content does not.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.4 for resistance against temperature, and Unit 1 for the first-order thermal lag that limits anemometer response speed.
chapters.leave: Humidity sensors as a family, MEMS flow sensors and SAW devices to Unit 5; ultrasonic, cup and vane anemometers to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Light and magnetic field both change the resistance of certain materials, giving two passive sensors with no moving parts.
chapters.depth: Photo-resistive sensor, also called a photoconductive cell or LDR: a serpentine film of cadmium sulphide or cadmium selenide on a ceramic substrate under a transparent window. Photons create electron-hole pairs, carrier density rises and resistance falls; recombination limits the speed to tens of milliseconds. Characteristics: dark resistance in the megohm range, light resistance of about 100 Ω to a few kilohm at 1000 lux, a law of the form R = A·E^(−γ) with γ between 0.5 and 1, a spectral peak near 540 nm for CdS, temperature dependence, and light-history memory. Applications: street-light switching, camera exposure, flame and burglar alarms, card readers. Magneto-resistive sensors: anisotropic magnetoresistance in permalloy thin films, a few percent, and giant magnetoresistance in multilayer stacks, tens of percent; the cause is spin-dependent scattering. Arrange the film as a four-arm bridge on chip to get a linear output against field, with a set/reset strap and a bias magnet. Applications: gear-tooth and cam position, wheel speed for ABS, current sensing, electronic compass, disk-drive heads.

figure.aria: One curve falling steeply from 100 kΩ at 10 lux to 1 kΩ at 1000 lux, showing that resistance and illuminance pull in opposite directions.
figure.caption: Resistance is inversely proportional to illuminance here: 10 kΩ at 100 lux, 1 kΩ at 1000 lux. The sensor is therefore much more sensitive in dim light than in bright light.

chapters.example: An LDR follows R = 10⁶/E with E in lux. (a) Find R at 100 lux. (b) The LDR is in series with a 10 kΩ fixed resistor across a 5 V supply, and the output is taken across the fixed resistor. Find the output at 100 lux. (c) Find R and the output at 500 lux. Answer: (a) R = 10⁶/100 = 10 kΩ. (b) the divider is 10 kΩ against 10 kΩ, so V_out = 5 × 10/(10 + 10) = 2.5 V. (c) R = 10⁶/500 = 2 kΩ; V_out = 5 × 10/(10 + 2) = 4.17 V.
chapters.trap: Treating the LDR as linear in lux and calibrating with one point. Also confusing a magneto-resistor, whose resistance changes, with a Hall sensor, whose voltage changes; the two are used for the same jobs but are different devices.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.2 for reading a small resistance change with a bridge, and Unit 1 for sensitivity and linearity.
chapters.leave: Photodiodes, phototransistors, photovoltaic and photoconductive-cell spectrophotometry, and the Hall effect, to Unit 4; GMR head construction and magnetic sensor materials to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Two dissimilar metals joined at two points generate an emf proportional to the temperature difference between the junctions, so the cold junction must be known or compensated.
chapters.depth: The Seebeck effect with the Peltier and Thomson effects; emf E = S(T_h − T_c) over a small span, with S the Seebeck coefficient in µV/°C. The three laws: homogeneous circuit (no emf from a single metal with a temperature gradient), intermediate metals (a third metal inserted at the same temperature changes nothing), and intermediate temperatures (E(T1,T3) = E(T1,T2) + E(T2,T3)). Standard types with approximate sensitivities and ranges: K chromel-alumel about 41 µV/°C, −200 °C to 1260 °C; J iron-constantan about 52 µV/°C, 0 °C to 750 °C; T copper-constantan about 43 µV/°C, −200 °C to 350 °C; E chromel-constantan about 68 µV/°C, the most sensitive; S and R platinum-rhodium about 10 µV/°C up to 1600 °C; B platinum-rhodium for the highest temperatures. Read from standard tables referred to 0 °C. Cold-junction compensation: ice bath, a compensating bridge with a thermistor in the terminal block, or software correction using a temperature sensor on the isothermal block. Matched extension and compensating leads. Characteristics: no excitation needed, self-powered, small and fast and rugged, cheap, but low output, nonlinear, needs amplification, and drifts if the cold junction drifts. Thermopiles and biomedical uses: skin and ear thermometry, heat-flux and respiration measurement.

figure.aria: A chain from the hot junction through the thermocouple wires to the cold junction on an isothermal block, then an amplifier, a stage that adds the cold-junction emf, and a display.
figure.caption: The cold junction never disappears — it only moves into the terminal block. Its own sensor supplies E(30 °C, 0 °C) = 1.20 mV, which is added to the measured 11.00 mV before the table lookup.

chapters.example: A K-type thermocouple gives 11.00 mV while its cold junction sits in an instrument terminal block at 30 °C. Standard tables give E(30 °C, 0 °C) = 1.20 mV. (a) Find the emf referred to 0 °C. (b) Find the hot-junction temperature. (c) Find the average sensitivity. Answer: (a) E(T_h, 0 °C) = 11.00 + 1.20 = 12.20 mV. (b) from the K-type table, 12.20 mV corresponds to about 300 °C. (c) 12.20 mV / 300 °C ≈ 41 µV/°C.
chapters.trap: Forgetting compensation, or subtracting the cold-junction emf when the law of intermediate temperatures says you add it. Also: copper wire in the cold junction creates two new junctions; use matched compensating cable, and keep both terminals at the same temperature.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.4 for comparison with RTDs and thermistors, and Unit 1 for the calibration chain and error analysis.
chapters.leave: Amplifier and isolation design for thermocouple front ends to Unit 6; radiation thermometry, thermopiles and IR detectors to Unit 4.
